title: Ga Kenkey
author: Fran Osseo-Asare
desc: Three cups of cornmeal soured three days, half of it cooked into aflata and recombined, wrapped in corn husks and steamed an hour.
longDesc: Kenkey is Ghana's great fermented staple and this is the Ga version — salted, wrapped in dried corn husks, shaped into balls. Three cups of white stone-ground cornmeal are mixed with about two and a half cups of warm water and left in a warm place, loosely covered, stirred well every day. Half the soured dough is then cooked with two cups of water and a teaspoon of salt for about ten minutes into a thick paste called aflata, the raw half is stirred back in, and the balls are wrapped in softened husks and steamed about an hour. The fermentation endpoint comes from the research literature, not from the recipe.
ingredients: 3 cups white stone-ground cornmeal — finely ground, not degerminated, not masa harina
About 2 1/2 cups warm water, plus more if the dough seems very dry
1 tbsp corn starch (optional, for a smoother dough)
Dried corn husks, softened in water
equipment: Steamer insert and a tall pot
Bowl of water, for wetting the hands
steps: Mix the cornmeal and the optional corn starch with the warm water in a nonreactive glass or ceramic container.
Keep it in a warm place, loosely covered, and stir well every day, removing any mould that forms on top or on the sides.
Ferment about 3 days in a cool kitchen — longer means more sour.

// ENDPOINT, from the research literature rather than this recipe: the dough is ready when it smells distinctly sour. Processors also watch for a change in colour. Dough fermented only 24 hours does not give a good-textured product, and three days is about the maximum.

Make the aflata: cook 2 cups of water, the salt and HALF the dough over medium heat about 10 minutes, stirring constantly with a heavy wooden spoon. It thickens in about 5 minutes and is quite thick by 10.
Remove from the heat and stir in the uncooked half.
Wet your hands and shape into 3 or 4 good-sized balls, tossing and turning each in one hand.
Wrap each ball in softened corn husks, overlapping at least a quarter inch over the previous husk, then twist the narrow ends together tightly and push the twisted end into the ball.
Steam on a steamer insert about an hour.
Let the balls cool slightly before unwrapping.
chefTips: The fermentation cue is NOT in this recipe and has to come from elsewhere. A survey of 138 kenkey processors found the readiness indicator was a SOUR SMELL for 63.8 per cent of them, and a change in colour for 34.1 per cent. That is the test to use.
Three days is about the maximum. The Ghanaian literature is explicit that dough fermented only 24 hours does not give a good-textured product, and that three days is the ceiling.
Stir every day and scrape off any mould. If you stir daily there usually is none — the stirring is what prevents it.

Corn husks, not foil or plastic. Her reasoning is worth having: foil does not let the balls steam properly, you lose the delicate corn husk flavour, and she worries about material transferring into the dough.
The aflata step — cooking half and folding in the raw half — is what gives kenkey its particular texture. Cooking all of it would give you banku.
White stone-ground cornmeal, finely ground, not degerminated, and definitely not masa harina. The source rules masa harina out explicitly.
She names and rejects the shortcut: adding a teaspoon of vinegar to unfermented dough to skip the wait. Her verdict is that it is cheating, and she is right — the flavour is not the same.
commonMistakes: Stopping at 24 hours, which gives poor texture.
Cooking all the dough instead of half.
Wrapping in foil instead of corn husks.
sources: QUANTITIES AND METHOD adapted from 'Recipe #12: Kenkey (Ghana's challenge to polenta)', betumiblog.blogspot.com, Wednesday 26 August 2009. BYLINE AS PRINTED: 'Posted by Fran at 7:54 AM'. BYLINE NOTE applying to every Betumi entry in this collection: every post prints 'Posted by Fran' — first name only — and no post examined prints 'Osseo-Asare'. The blog is Fran Osseo-Asare's, founded 1997, and betumi.com carries the site-level line 'Content/Images © Fran Osseo-Asare', so the attribution is secure though the per-post byline is a first name.

COMMUNITY, from the author: 'I prefer Ga-style kenkey because I first lived in Nungua along the coast of Ghana'. She describes the Fante style as the one 'which has no salt, is steamed in plantain leaves and formed into a different shape' — see GHA038.

Ingredients as printed, TWO-PASS across three fetches: '3 cups of cornmeal/flour this time'; optional 'a tablespoon of corn starch if you wish to make it a little smoother'; 'about 2 1/2 cups of warm water'. For the aflata: '2 cups of water', 'a teaspoon of salt (or less)', 'half of the dough'. SINGLE-PASS detail: the cornmeal is white, stone ground, finely ground, not degerminated, not masa harina; the water carries a parenthetical '(plus more if dough seems very dry)'; the wrapping is dried corn husks. YIELD, SINGLE-PASS: '3 or 4 good-sized balls'.
HYDRATION CHECK: no misprint. 3 cups meal to 2½ cups water is a stiff paste, and 2 further cups go into the aflata.

THE FERMENTATION INSTRUCTION AS PRINTED, verbatim and TWO-PASS: 'Keep it in a warm place, loosely covered and stir well every day, removing any mold that forms on top or on the sides'. And: 'As with Ethiopian injera batter, the longer you let the dough sit, the more sour it will be.' And: 'I let mine sit for about 3 days here in central Pennsylvania, which has a cooler climate than Ghana's.'

THIS RECIPE HAS NO REAL FERMENTATION DONENESS CUE, and that is stated plainly. Its only cue is relative — more days means more sour. There is no sourness target, no smell, no pH, no rise and no bubble cue. Her stopping rule is the number of days she personally used in a cooler climate. Her only observable fermentation signal is mould, which she says to remove. UNDER THIS COLLECTION'S RULE THAT WOULD MAKE THE DISH UNPUBLISHABLE; what makes it publishable is the research literature below, which supplies the endpoint her recipe lacks. The two halves are attributed separately and the step list marks which is which.

THE ENDPOINT, from a processor survey and therefore genuine practice: Abdul-Samed R., 'Modelling and Optimisation of the Fanti Kenkey Production Process', MPhil thesis, University of Ghana, surveying 138 Fante kenkey processors. TWO-PASS verbatim: the readiness indicator for '88 respondents or 63.8%, was a sour smell, while 47 respondents or 34.1% noted a change in colour.' Fermentation duration among them: one day 35.5%, two days 34.1%, three days 22.5%. Room temperature given SINGLE-PASS as '28±2°C'. CAVEAT: the thesis notes pH 'showed no significant correlation with texture variables or processing factors'.

THE TEXTURE LIMITS, from Amoa-Awua W.K.A. and Oduro-Yeboah C., 'African Food Tradition Revisited by Research: Kenkey – Background Information and Literature Review', CSIR Food Research Institute. ALL TWO-PASS. Verbatim: 'Dough fermented for 24h does not give a good-textured product'. And: 'Three days seem to be the maximum time for the fermentation.' Ga kenkey specifically is 'fermented for 2-3 days, salted, cooked, wrapped in maize husks and has a shelf-life of about 3 to 4 days'. Process: 'allowed to ferment spontaneously for up to 3 days at ambient temperature (i.e., 25–30 °C)'. Product pH: 'Both are cooked sour tasting stiff porridges with a pH of about 3.7'.

FOR ANYONE WITH pH STRIPS, the industrial critical limits, from Amoa-Awua W.K.A., Ngunjiri P., Anlobe J., Kpodo K., Halm M., Jakobsen M., 'Experiences in the Application of HACCP to Traditional Food Processing at a Semi-Commercial Kenkey Production Plant in Accra, Ghana'. TWO-PASS: steeping at 24 h 'pH 4.2+ 0.1'; dough fermentation 'pH not> 3.9', titratable acidity 1.4-2% lactic and 0.18-0.23% acetic. Both steps monitored by 'Visual inspection' and 'Use of pH strips'. Verification batches at 48 h dough: pH 3.73 with 1.41% acidity, and pH 3.75 with 1.47%. Cooking not less than 3 h. QUALITY CHECK, verbatim: the dough 'was examined for pH, odour and mould growth on the surface', and good fermentation shows 'a drop in pH to levels indicating rapid growth of lactic acid bacteria' and 'the absence of offensive odour'. CAUTION: one fetch rendered the fermentation time as 't18 h', an OCR error; the verification table and the other fetch say 48 h. THIS IS A SEMI-COMMERCIAL PLANT RUNNING THE TRADITIONAL PROCESS, not a lab fermentation.

pH FROM COMMERCIAL PRODUCTION SAMPLES: Jespersen L., Halm M., Kpodo K., Jakobsen M., 'The significance of yeasts and moulds occurring in maize dough fermentation for "kenkey" production', International Journal of Food Microbiology, 1994, sampling 'two larger commercial production sites and four markets in Accra'. Verbatim: 'The pH of the fresh dough was around 5.7 falling rapidly below pH 4.0'. Table values, with the two fetches disagreeing: 24 h gives pH 3.7-4.1 (both agree); 48 h gives 3.5-3.7 on one fetch and 3.5-3.8 for 48-72 h combined on the other; 72 h gives 3.7-3.8 on one fetch. Treat it as approximately pH 3.5-3.8 at 48-72 h. Organisms: Candida krusei and Saccharomyces cerevisiae above 10^6 cfu/g (single pass).

A CONTROLLED STUDY WHOSE NUMBERS DO NOT MATCH THE OTHERS, recorded unreconciled: Bugyei G.K., Affrifah N.S., Joye I., Lim L.T., Essien E., Duizer L., Apalangya V.A., Harrison O.A., Cao W., Ahenkorah C.K., Singh S.S., Saalia F.K., 'Effects of corn dough fermentation on the physicochemical, starch microstructural, and rheological properties of Ga kenkey, a fermented corn dumpling', International Journal of Food Properties, 2026, DOI 10.1080/10942912.2026.2654301. ABSTRACT ONLY, reached via a University of Ghana repository record; the full text was not read. TWO-PASS: 'pH ... from 6.12 ± 0.01 to 4.32 ± 0.01 after 72 h fermentation'; fermentation at '28 °C for 24, 48, and 72 h'; conclusion that a 'fermentation period of 48 h is sufficient to produce acceptable Ga kenkey', with 72 h described as traditional. ITS 72-HOUR pH OF 4.32 IS MUCH HIGHER than the pH 3.5-3.8 every production and market study reports. That discrepancy is not resolved here, and the 24 h and 48 h pH values were not obtained.

OTHER FIGURES, for completeness. Amoa-Awua, Anlobe, Hodasi 1996 (SINGLE-PASS): spontaneous control pH 6.15 falling to 3.81 over 48 h at 30 °C; verbatim 'the final level of pH i.e. 3.7, expected in maize dough fermented spontaneously for 48 h'. Halm et al. 1996: 'in most inoculated doughs the required pH was attained by 24 h instead of 48 h', with taste panels REJECTING 24 h kenkey and accepting 48 h starter-fermented kenkey. Kpodo 2004 processor survey: in the Coastal Scrub zone 12 of 15 processors fermented the dough 3 days; in other zones 57 of 60 fermented 1 day only. FAO's 'Fermented cereals: a global perspective' gives kenkey dough as fermenting '72 hr' and names 'obligatively heterofermentative lactobacilli related to L. fermentum and L. reuteri', but contains NO pH or acidity numbers.

HER OTHER TIPS, as printed. On aflatoxin: 'don't worry about aflatoxins--name brands of corn flour will have been properly processed'. On foil: 'The foil does not allow the balls to steam in properly, and also you lose the wonderful delicate flavor of the corn husks. Plus I worry about the transfer of unwanted materials from the foil or plastic into the dough itself.' On the vinegar shortcut, which she rejects: 'Some people say that if you don't want to wait for the dough to sour, you can just add a teaspoon or so of vinegar to the unfermented dough and use it immediately, but I feel like that's cheating.'

COOKING, as printed: 'I simply put a steamer insert into a stainless steel pot with water and place the balls on top and steam them for about an hour.' Also: 'In Ghana I was actually taught to put corn husks in the bottom of the pot and fill it with water, then boil the balls for a couple of hours.' And: 'When removing the balls from the pot (it usually takes mine a good hour), be sure to let them cool slightly before unwrapping them.' NOTE the two methods give very different times — an hour steamed against a couple of hours boiled — and both are hers.
ACCOMPANIMENTS she names: 'seasoned fried fish ("kenan" or "kyenam")', 'a fresh hot pepper sauce' and 'the classic "shito"'.

WITHIN-AUTHOR DISAGREEMENT across her three fermented posts, recorded and not averaged: kenkey about 3 days with a relative sourness cue only; banku 'several days' WITH a bubbling cue and 'probably 2 days' for a first attempt (GHA041); akple described as unfermented corn dough (GHA042).
storage: 3 to 4 days, per the literature on Ga kenkey. Refrigerate or freeze and thaw — her own note is that they are best warm.
reheating: Re-steam in the husks, or microwave wrapped in damp paper.
healthBenefits: Fermentation raises B-vitamin availability and reduces phytate, improving mineral absorption.
The lactic acid bacteria involved are documented probiotic genera.
The low final pH acts as a natural preservative.
culturalNote: Kenkey is sold wrapped in its husks from basins all over Accra and eaten with fried fish and shito in the hand, standing up. The Ga and Fante versions are different foods that share a name — salted and husk-wrapped against unsalted and plantain-leaf-wrapped — and people have firm views about which is correct depending on where they are from.
